_comment: Plan-reading configuration. This file holds only project-level VOCABULARY and THRESHOLDS that an office may legitimately tune for its own drawing conventions - room names, title-block labels, wall thicknesses, tolerances. No extracted answer, coordinate or count from any particular plan belongs here or anywhere in the code. Editing an entry below retunes the reader for a different office without changing any code.

confidence_thresholds._comment: A value at or above 'review' is shown as confirmed; between 'low' and 'review' it is shown as needing review; below 'low' it is shown as low-confidence and raised as an unresolved item.

title_block._comment: Labels printed beside or above a title-block value. Matched as a whole line, case-insensitively, ignoring a trailing ':' or '.'. 'page_specific' labels identify THIS sheet; 'project_wide' labels identify the whole job and are recorded separately, never used as a sheet identifier (a project number repeated on all 6 sheets is not a sheet number).
title_block._sheet_title_note: Used only when no title label is printed on the sheet. A line containing one of these drawing-type phrases is a strong sheet-title candidate. 'DETAIL' is deliberately absent: it appears constantly inside ordinary note sentences ('refer to detail 3'), which made it a measured source of false titles.
title_block._title_exclusion_note: Phrases that are page furniture rather than a sheet title. Applied ONLY to the last-resort guess; a title found from a printed label or from the sheet_title_keywords allowlist above is never overruled by this list (a sheet legitimately titled 'DOOR SCHEDULE SHT.1' must not be discarded for containing the word 'SCHEDULE').

sheet_index._comment: Most Australian plan sets print a drawing index on the cover sheet listing every sheet's number, title, scale and revision. Parsing it gives an independent, in-document reference to cross-check every sheet's own title block against — this is what turns a detected value into a verified one instead of an unchecked guess.
sheet_index._min_numbered_row_share_note: A drawing index lists other sheets, and nearly every row of one prints a drawing number. A row without one is real and is kept - a cover sheet often has none - but a table where most rows have no number is not an index. Without this test, a title block printed as a row of labels across the top of a sheet reads as an index header, and the rows collected below it are the drawing's own room names and dimensions.

page_types._comment: requires plan/elevation pages to be identified. A page's type is decided from its detected sheet title first (the drawing says what it is), then from the strongest keyword evidence in the page body. Each entry lists the phrases that indicate that type, most specific first.
page_types._floor_plan_evidence_note: A page claiming to be a floor plan is confirmed by real floor-plan evidence: several room labels plus dimension strings. Where the title says one thing and the content says another, both are reported and the disagreement is flagged rather than silently resolved.
page_types._plan_evidence_note: A sheet may carry a plan under a title that names something else - one office titles a sheet 'FRAMING SPECIFICATIONS' and prints a full floor plan on it. Room labels and dimensions then promote it to a plan so that walls are looked for. A title that names an elevation, section, detail or schedule is never promoted: those sheets print room names and dimensions as well, and parallel lines on them are window frames and hatching, not walls.
page_types._min_rooms_with_dimensions_note: A small building - an extension, a granny flat, a shed - prints only two or three room names. Requiring four before a sheet counts as a plan meant its only floor plan was never recognised as one. A sheet with fewer rooms but a full set of dimensions beside them counts as a plan as well.
page_types._caption_note: Many offices print a generic project title in the title block and name the drawing in large type under the drawing itself. That caption is used when the title block names no kind of drawing. Only captions at least this share of the largest matching type on the sheet are considered, so a small section marker beside a cutting line - which refers to another sheet - cannot decide what this sheet is.
page_types._level_marker_note: Printed height levels (RL, FFL, NGL, AHD) are how a drawing states a height. A sheet with this many of them and no room names is a drawing of the building seen from the side or cut through, never a plan.
page_types._sentence_share_note: The share of a sheet's lines that read as written sentences rather than drawing labels. Above this, with no dimensions on the sheet, it is a notes or specification sheet.
page_types._roof_plan_note: A roof plan is drawn looking down like a floor plan, but it shows the roof: its parallel lines are battens, ridges, valleys and gutter lines, not walls, and it names no rooms. Keeping it apart from floor plans stops 200 roof lines being reported as walls of the building.

discipline._comment: Discipline is taken from the sheet number's letter prefix first (an AU drawing convention), then from the page type, and only then from a discipline word printed on the sheet. A discipline word found inside a drawing index or a consultant's letterhead describes another sheet, not this one, so those regions are excluded before this fallback runs.

rooms._comment: Room detection uses two independent methods and records which one found each room. (1) Vocabulary: the label matches a known Australian residential room name. (2) Geometry: a short label with a paired dimension printed directly beneath it in the same column is a room callout by drawing convention, whatever it is called — this is what lets an unseen plan's unusual room name ('MULTI-FUNCTION') still be found without adding it to any list.
rooms._exclusion_note: Text that contains a room word but describes a fixture, finish or note rather than a room.
rooms._geometric_note: A candidate room label found geometrically must be short, mostly letters, and have a paired dimension printed within this many multiples of its own height directly below it.
rooms._geometric_size_note: A label with a paired dimension beneath it is only a room if that dimension is a room-sized one. Without these limits a timber section note (90 x 32) and a ceiling hatch (600 x 600) were both reported as rooms. A label matched by name is unaffected: a named room is a room whether or not a size is printed.
rooms._element_words_note: A label that names a building element is a note on the drawing, not a room, even when a room word appears inside it: 'PROPOSED DECK ROOF SHEETING' is not the DECK. Elevations and specification sheets are full of these. Add an office's own wording here; no code change is needed.
rooms._max_extra_words_note: How many words a room label may carry beyond the vocabulary name it matched. 'REAR DECK' and 'MASTER BEDROOM' are room labels; 'PROPOSED DECK ROOF SHEETING' is a sentence that merely mentions one.

dimensions._comment: Australian residential drawings write dimensions in millimetres by default. A bare number with no unit is only accepted as a dimension when the printed line is essentially just that number and it falls inside a buildable range; anything else is left as ordinary text rather than invented as a measurement.
dimensions.assumed_unit_note: Bare numbers with no unit suffix are read as millimetres per Australian residential drawing convention. This assumption is recorded on every such record and is never presented as a confirmed unit.
dimensions._chain_note: Dimensions printed along one line form a dimension string. Where the drawing also prints the total for that string, the individual figures must add up to it: that is a real arithmetic test of the extraction and uses the tight tolerance below. Two separate strings that happen to span the same distance are compared as well, but with a wider tolerance, because two strings can legitimately measure to different faces of the same wall and differ by a wall thickness.
dimensions._overall_note: Words a drawing prints beside the total run of a dimension chain.
dimensions._association_note: A dimension is only linked to a room or an opening mark when the geometry supports it: the label must lie in the direction the dimension measures and within this many multiples of the dimension's own text height. An unlinked dimension is reported as unlinked — a wrong link is worse than none, because downstream stages trust it (the project rules/5).
dimensions._level_note: Elevation and section sheets print reduced levels (RL) rather than plan dimensions.
dimensions._measured_to_note: Notes an office may print after a dimension figure saying what it measures to - '10260 TO WALL', '2600 TO EAVE', '900 CLEAR'. The figure is read as the measurement and the note is kept alongside it, never dropped. Add an office's own wording here; no code changes are needed.

openings._comment: Door and window marks used on Australian residential plans. The prefix decides the element type; the number is the mark's instance. Extend this list for an office that uses different marks — nothing else in the pipeline needs changing.
openings._standard_note: Plausible overall opening widths, used only to sanity-check an extracted width and flag an implausible one. Never used to fill in a missing value. The door range covers a single leaf through to a wide sliding/stacker or robe unit, which are measured as one opening on Australian residential schedules.
openings._linking_note: A mark is placed on a candidate wall only when one wall is clearly the closest: the mark must sit within the wall run, within the distance below, and no other wall may be within this ratio of that distance. Where two walls are equally close the opening is reported without a wall and the reason is given.

schedules._comment: Door/window/finishes schedules are real tables. Their header row is found by matching printed column headers below, then every row beneath is read by column position — so the schedule's actual contents are extracted, not merely the fact that the word 'SCHEDULE' appeared somewhere.

legends._comment: A legend maps a drawn symbol or hatch to its meaning. Only the printed entries are captured; no universal symbol library is assumed (explicitly out of scope for this release).

overlay._comment: Colours used to draw detected items over the source page render, so a reviewer can see false positives and misses directly. Each category is drawn in a distinct colour and listed in the on-image legend.

ocr._comment: Settings for reading scanned (image-only) sheets. OCR runs only on pages that have no usable text layer of their own; a page with real text is never OCR’d, so a vector plan set is unaffected by anything here. Measured on this machine: one dense A3 construction sheet at 150 DPI takes about 230 seconds and returns roughly 400 text items at 0.89–1.00 recognition confidence. The default budget below is set above that so a scanned sheet actually completes; lower it for a faster run that gives up sooner, raise it for larger or denser sheets. A page that exceeds the budget is reported as timed out, never silently returned empty.
ocr._render_dpi_note: The resolution the page is rendered at before OCR. Higher reads small text more reliably but costs proportionally more time.
ocr._run_budget_note: Total seconds of OCR allowed across one upload. A scanned set of many sheets would otherwise run for over an hour with the browser showing nothing. When the budget is used up, the remaining pages are read from whatever text they have and each says plainly that it was not read by OCR - never silently returned as empty.
ocr._text_layer_note: A PDF stores which glyph to draw; recording what that glyph means is optional, and plotting software and older CAD exports often leave it out. The sheet then carries plenty of text that is not the wording printed on it. Counting characters cannot tell the difference, so the text itself is judged: a sheet that fails either test below is treated as having no text of its own, is read from its page image instead, and says so on screen. Measured across the drawings in use, the lowest share of letters and digits on any sheet is 0.90 and none contains an unreadable character, so these settings sit far away from anything a real drawing produces.
ocr._picture_drawing_note: A sheet can carry a full title block as real text while its whole drawing is a picture placed beside it. The sheet then has plenty of characters and looks fully readable, yet every room name and dimension inside the picture is unread. The test is where the characters are, not how many: a large picture with almost nothing printed inside it is a drawing nobody has read. Text lines per 100x100 points of picture is the measure - every sheet in use that carries its own text prints between 0.41 and 2.85 that way, so the default sits well clear of all of them.

scale_calibration._comment: The printed scale is checked against the drawing own dimension strings before anything is measured with it. Each figure in a string is centred on the segment it describes, so the distance between the first and last figure centres is known from the printed numbers alone and can be compared with the distance measured on the page. A sheet that disagrees by more than the tolerance is flagged and its lengths are not used.
scale_calibration._agreement_note: The individual strings must also agree with each other before any conclusion is drawn. Where they do not, the result is 'inconclusive' rather than 'contradicted': one badly grouped string is not evidence that the printed scale is wrong.

walls._comment: A wall is drawn as two parallel lines a wall thickness apart. Repeated and broken-up drawings of the same line are merged into one face first, then each face is paired with its nearest plausible partner and only if that partner nearest is the same face, so one wall produces one record. These are candidates for review, not confirmed walls.
walls._nominal_note: Wall thicknesses this office actually builds. A measured thickness close to one of these is a stronger candidate. The measured value is always kept as measured; the nominal one is reported alongside it as context.
walls._scope_note: Walls are looked for only on sheets that draw the building in plan: the page type must be listed below AND the sheet must label at least this many rooms. Two parallel lines a wall thickness apart mean a wall on a floor plan; on an elevation they are a window frame, and on a roof plan they are battens and flashings.
walls._merge_note: A wall face is interrupted wherever a door or window sits in it, so the drawing contains it as several collinear pieces. Pieces on the same line separated by less than this are joined into one face: a wall with a window in it is still one wall. Without this the longest wall found on a 20 m building was 6 m.
walls._pairing_note: Faces are paired by how far they run together, not by which is nearest. A long external wall has many lines near it — linings, hatching, joinery — and the nearest one is rarely its own other face. The longest shared run wins, a nominal thickness breaks ties, and each face belongs to one wall only.
walls._length_allowance_comment: A wall may run a little past the point a dimension string measures to, so a candidate is kept up to this multiple of the longest distance the sheet itself measures. Anything longer is not a wall of this building - it is the block boundary or an eave line - and is set aside as an item to check.
walls._opening_flank_comment: A break in a wall counts as a door or window only when this much wall is drawn on both sides of it. A break running to the end of a wall is where the wall meets another wall, or where the drawing stopped - not an opening.
walls._never_trace_walls_on_note: Sheet kinds whose parallel lines are not walls. A site plan draws the block: its parallel lines are boundaries, setbacks, easements, fences and driveways, and at site-plan scale a wall is about one point thick, so nothing measured off it would be a wall thickness. Reporting those as walls would bury the real ones from the floor plan.
walls._unnamed_plan_note: How many rooms a sheet names says nothing about whether it is a plan: an extension, a granny flat, a studio or a shed names two or three, and a plan drawn without room names names none. So walls are looked for first and the result is judged. Where the sheet says it is a plan - in its title block or in its own caption - the walls found are the walls. Where the kind was only inferred from what is printed, the drawing must look like a building first: a building is a closed shape, so at least this many walls, and at least this share of them at a thickness the office actually builds.

accuracy._comment: Tolerances used when comparing a run against tests/ground_truth.csv. A row in that file may override them with its own tolerance_pct. Text values are compared exactly; numeric ones within the tolerance below.
accuracy._targets_note: These are the bars The reader on the agreed test area; they are reported, never enforced by silently adjusting anything.

raster_lines._comment: Not every plan set is vector. One supplied set places its drawing on the page as embedded images with only text as real geometry, so its wall lines cannot be read from the PDF's own paths. A sheet whose own geometry yields no walls has its lines recovered from the rendered page instead, and every wall records which source it came from.

model._comment: Settings for turning read plan data into the canonical building model. A floor plan cannot show height, so the drawing set is asked for it two ways - the figure the sections dimension, and the distance between the printed levels - and the two are compared. Only when neither answers is the default below used, and the model then says on its face that every height in it is an assumption.

storey_height_mm._note: The buildable range a storey height must fall in, and the office default for when the drawing states none. 2700 is a common Australian residential ceiling height; change it to whatever this office builds.

model._height_repeats_note: A section dimensions the same storey several times over. A figure in the height range printed only once is a window head or a door, not the storey.
model._floor_level_note: Prefixes an office uses for a floor level. Every other level prefix (CL, FCL, RL) is treated as a level above it, and the difference is a candidate storey height.
model._default_thickness_note: Used only when a wall's own thickness could not be measured. Every wall records whether its thickness was measured or defaulted.
model._min_wall_length_note: A candidate shorter than this is not carried into the model; at drawing scale it is a jamb, a step in a wall face or a fragment, not a wall to build.

rendering._comment: How large a page image the machine reading the plan is willing to hold. Drawing sizes are not bounded, and a very large sheet rendered at full resolution can need more memory than a small server has, which ends the run part way through. A sheet larger than this allowance is rendered at a lower resolution instead - never cropped - and the reduction is recorded. An A3 or A1 sheet is nowhere near this limit; raise it on a larger machine if very big drawings need to be read at full detail.

tables._comment: A schedule, a legend and a drawing index are panels printed on a sheet; the drawing occupies the rest of it. The area a table covers is excluded from room and dimension detection, so a table read wrongly can swallow the drawing. A table claiming more than this share of the sheet is not a table, and is dropped rather than allowed to hide the drawing behind it.
